slides.title: Chapter 1: Introduction
slides.say: This chapter answers one question: what is Bitcoin, and why does every part of it exist? The cover shows a gold coin on circuit traces, a picture from the owner's 2025 Chapter 1 deck. Common first answers are that Bitcoin is an app or a company. The better answer, developed over the next 75 slides, is that it is a shared ledger of who owns what, kept by many computers under common rules. Every result on a slide was computed with Python 3.14.6 and not typed, and the same code runs on the course page.
slides.takeaway: What Bitcoin is, what it is made of, and why every part of it exists

slides.title: Today's route through six parts
slides.say: Six parts follow the order that a first payment needs them: origins, money and price, the network, wallets and keys, a first payment and foundations, followed by a summary, resources and a close. Each number in the list is a range of slides. The three counters on the right show what the chapter contains: 76 slides, nine true stories that each carry a source link, and fifteen code examples that each show a picture of their result. Every example also appears in the Run slide code tab of the course page, where it can be run and compared with the slide.
slides.takeaway: Six parts, fifteen examples, nine true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: The chapter is organised around six questions, and each has its answer on a slide. The summary returns to them at the end. They cover where Bitcoin came from and what it combined, what the unit of its money is and who decides how much exists, who sets the price and how a double-spend is refused, how wallets differ and who controls the keys, what an address and an invoice are and how a wallet sends with change, and what payment channels can do that the chain alone cannot. A first answer to the first question often lists inventors; the better answer is that Bitcoin combined four earlier parts, shown in part 2.
slides.takeaway: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

slides.title: One chapter, six branches
slides.say: The map is the skeleton of the chapter: one root and six branches, which are money, network, wallet, usage, foundations and nature. Every slide belongs to one branch, and each part of the deck opens by returning to this map. The names under a branch list the ideas that its slides explain, for example unit, supply, price and issuance under money, or consensus, history and standards under network. The course page carries the same map as a figure that can be clicked, so a reader can jump from a branch to its explanations.
slides.takeaway: Six branches; every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: Origins: three beats of the story
slides.say: Origins has three beats. The first block, block 0, carries a newspaper headline dated 3 January 2009. The first payment followed nine days later, when Satoshi Nakamoto sent ten bitcoin to Hal Finney. Forty years of earlier work came before both: Chaum, Back, Dai and Szabo each built one part of what Bitcoin later combined. The headline is not decoration; it is a dated proof that the block was not made earlier. Slides 7 to 11 tell these three beats in order, and the strip at the bottom shows where this part sits in the chapter.
slides.takeaway: Bitcoin combines parts that existed before it.

slides.title: Origins: the key concepts
slides.say: Two cards open the chapter. The introduction states what Bitcoin is and why it matters, and the history of Bitcoin traces the path from earlier digital money to the first block in January 2009. The strip at the bottom shows where this part sits among the six parts of the chapter. A common mistake is to learn the history as a list of dates. The slides that follow show instead which part of Bitcoin each earlier system built, and why none of them could work without the others.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A newspaper headline carved into block zero
slides.say: On 3 January 2009 Satoshi Nakamoto mined block 0, the first block of the Bitcoin chain. The script of the block contains the headline of The Times of that day. The headline proves that the block was not made earlier, and it records the banking crisis that Bitcoin answers. The hex dump on the slide shows the bytes, and the source link opens the same block on a block explorer, so anyone can check it today. A common mistake is to read the headline as a message to the public; its purpose is a timestamp that stays verifiable. The next slide reads those 69 bytes with code.
slides.takeaway: Recorded: 3 January 2009

slides.title: The headline inside block zero
slides.say: The code cuts the script of block 0 into its first eight bytes, which are pushes, and the text that follows. The result [8, 69] adds up to the 77 bytes of the whole script, and the table beside the code shows the same split. Decoding the remaining 69 bytes as text gives the Times headline of 3 January 2009. Bytes become text only after they are decoded, which is why the code decodes the slice that holds the headline and not the whole script: the first eight bytes hold numbers, not text.
slides.takeaway: The first block carries its own date: a newspaper headline

slides.title: The first person ever paid in bitcoin
slides.say: Nine days after block 0, on 12 January 2009, Satoshi Nakamoto sent 10 bitcoin to the cryptographer Hal Finney in block 170, the first payment between two people. Finney had answered the white paper with curiosity and had built the first reusable proof-of-work system years before. He ran the software and wrote 'Running bitcoin'. The coins reached him directly, with no bank in between, so the first payment already shows the whole idea: two people and one shared ledger. A common mistake is to call Finney the first miner; he ran the software and received the coins.
slides.takeaway: Satoshi Nakamoto, and the cryptographer who ran the code

slides.title: Forty years of failed digital money
slides.say: Between 1982 and 1998 David Chaum, Adam Back, Wei Dai and Nick Szabo each built a part of digital money. Their systems failed or stayed unbuilt, because none of them could agree on one history without a trusted leader. Satoshi Nakamoto's white paper of 31 October 2008 cites them and adds proof of work as the voting weight of an open network. The photograph shows David Chaum, and the link opens the white paper. A common mistake is to say that Bitcoin invented digital cash. It was a new combination of four near misses.
slides.takeaway: Every part existed before Bitcoin combined them

slides.title: Four near misses, one combination
slides.say: The timeline runs from 1982 to 2009: Chaum's ecash in 1982, Back's Hashcash in 1997, Dai's b-money and Szabo's bit gold in 1998, Nakamoto's white paper in 2008 and the first block in 2009. DigiCash went bankrupt, and b-money and bit gold were never built. What the four near misses lacked was agreement on one history without a leader. The pieces were old and the combination was new. The dates are easy to mix up, so it helps to remember five anchors: 1982, 1997, 1998, 2008 and 2009.
slides.takeaway: The pieces were old; the combination was new

slides.title: Money and price in three beats
slides.say: Money is a ledger of who owns what, and Bitcoin keeps that ledger in public. This part has three beats: what money was, units and supply, and price and exchange. Stones, coins, notes and bank balances are all ledgers. One bitcoin divides into 100 million satoshis and the cap is 21 million. Markets set the price, and exchanges and ATMs convert it. Slides 14 to 19 cover money as a ledger, slides 20 to 23 units and supply, and slides 24 to 27 price. A bank balance is a ledger too, kept privately by the bank.
slides.takeaway: Money is a ledger of who owns what; Bitcoin keeps that ledger in public.

slides.title: Money and price: key concepts
slides.say: Four cards define the vocabulary of price. A floating exchange rate is a price set by markets that moves with supply and demand. Finding the current price means reading exchange quotes, where a volume-weighted average gives one fair daily figure. A currency exchange is a market where buyers and sellers swap bitcoin and local money, with identity checks. A Bitcoin ATM takes cash and sends bitcoin to a phone wallet. Students often think that someone sets the price of bitcoin; the next slides show that trades do.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: The island where money never moved
slides.say: On the island of Yap, wealth was held in limestone discs called rai, some four metres wide, that did not move when they changed owner. The anthropologist William Henry Furness III described this after visiting in 1903, and a stone that sank at sea was still traded. What changed was the shared memory of who owned each stone, so the stones worked as a public ledger. The photograph shows a rai stone. A common mistake is to focus on the size of the stones instead of the record of ownership.

read.label: Furness: The Island of Stone Money (book)

slides.takeaway: Documented in 1903; the free ebook edition came in 2024

slides.title: Five thousand years to digital cash
slides.say: Grain ledgers, Lydian coins, paper notes and bank balances are all ledgers, and they differ only in who keeps them. On 15 August 1971 President Richard Nixon cut the dollar's last tie to gold, leaving pure fiat money. Cards and online banking then made money digital as entries in private ledgers, and Bitcoin keeps the ledger in public. The photograph shows an electrum stater of 600 to 550 BCE, and the link leads to a money museum's history of money. A common slip is to say that fiat money has no ledger; bank balances are one.
slides.takeaway: From grain ledgers to pure fiat money, 3000 BCE to 1971

slides.title: Traditional, digital, crypto: side by side
slides.say: This is the chapter's one comparison table. Its columns are traditional cash, digital money held in banks, cards and e-money, and cryptocurrency. Its rows give who issues the money, how it exists, who keeps the ledger, what sets the supply and how it settles. The three kinds of money serve the same uses but differ in who keeps the ledger: cash has none because possession is the record, banks keep private ledgers, and Bitcoin's nodes keep one public ledger together. Bitcoin settles in about an hour, not instantly.
slides.takeaway: Same uses, different ledgers: that difference is this course

slides.title: The internet got payments - and new gatekeepers
slides.say: On 8 July 2002 eBay agreed to buy PayPal for 1.5 billion dollars, ending the dot-com race to pay online. PayPal grew from Confinity, founded by Max Levchin and Peter Thiel in 1998, and X.com, founded by Elon Musk in 1999, which merged in 2000. Beenz and Flooz died in the 2001 crash. Online payment had been solved only as accounts on one company's private ledger, so the internet still had no cash: every payment passed through a gatekeeper who could say no. A common mistake is to treat online payment as digital cash.
slides.takeaway: The dot-com boom digitised paying, not cash

slides.title: When the money in your hand stops working
slides.say: On 26 February 2022 the government of Ukraine, through Mykhailo Fedorov's ministry of digital transformation, published cryptocurrency donation addresses. With an aid group it raised 54.7 million dollars in about a week, and CNBC reported the total on 3 March 2022. With war at the capital, ordinary payment rails were too slow, while an open network kept working. Donors needed only an address to send help from anywhere. The figures should be checked in the CNBC source linked on the slide and not repeated from memory.
slides.takeaway: Ukraine, February 2022: a state turns to an open payment network

slides.title: When the money in your hand stops working
slides.say: Five documented cases show what happens when the money in hand stops working. Kenya in 2007 had no bank access for most adults, and M-Pesa made phones the payment rail. Cyprus in 2013 closed its banks for days while a levy took part of deposits overnight. Greece in 2015 capped ATM withdrawals at 60 euros a day. Venezuela in 2018 had hyperinflation beyond 1,000,000 percent. Ukraine in 2022 raised 54.7 million dollars in cryptocurrency in a week. Each case has its own photograph and link, and none is hypothetical. Some cases are about trust in banks and others about access.
slides.takeaway: Crisis or war, banked or not: the need is documented

slides.title: A bitcoin counted in satoshis
slides.say: A bitcoin is counted in whole satoshis, one hundred million to the coin. The code converts 0.001 bitcoin exactly with the Decimal type and lists three common amounts as counts of satoshis: 100,000,000, 100,000 and 1, as the result shows. Exact whole numbers matter for money because floating-point numbers store most decimals only approximately. A common mistake is to type 0.001 as a float and multiply it, which gives no guarantee of an exact count.
slides.takeaway: Money here is counting, and the units are exact

slides.title: The subsidy at five block heights
slides.say: The subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks. The code evaluates it at five heights, 0, 210,000, 420,000, 630,000 and 840,000, and the result is 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 3.125 bitcoin. The chart shows the same five values, and the second code line confirms that each era pays exactly half of the era before it. The next value would be half of 3.125. A common mistake is to think that halving happens on a date; it happens at a block height, and the era of 3.125 bitcoin began in April 2024.
slides.takeaway: Every halving cuts new issuance in half

slides.title: The 21 million cap is a sum
slides.say: The cap of 21 million bitcoin is a sum of every era's issuance. Each era issues its subsidy for 210,000 blocks, then the subsidy halves, and the code adds the 33 eras that still issue at least one satoshi per block. The result, 20,999,999.9769 bitcoin, is just under 21 million because each halving drops any fraction below one satoshi. The chart shows the total creeping toward the cap. Scarcity here is arithmetic that every node can run again, not a promise made by anyone.
slides.takeaway: Scarcity is arithmetic that every node can re-run

slides.title: A central bank's jobs, done by rules
slides.say: A central bank decides how much money exists, and a clearing house settles payments; Bitcoin does both by rule. The table maps three institutional jobs to the rules that every node checks. Mining takes over the issuing and clearing work, so no central bank is needed for the currency to work. The word deflationary describes a supply whose issuance shrinks and ends. It is a tendency of the supply and does not promise that the price will rise.
slides.takeaway: Rules every node checks replace three institutions' jobs

slides.title: Where a price comes from
slides.say: A price is the last place where a buyer and a seller agreed. The ladder shows toy bids below and asks above the market, in bitcoin per price level. Here the best bid is 62,000 and the best ask is 62,100, so nothing trades until one side moves. When a buyer raises the bid to the ask, a trade happens, and that trade becomes the last price. An exchange quotes such a price, and a Bitcoin ATM adds a margin. The numbers on the ladder are illustrative.
slides.takeaway: A price is the last place a buyer and a seller agreed

slides.title: No one sets the price: trades do
slides.say: A price is a ratio, and a day's figure is a weighted average. The code lists three illustrative trades as bitcoin bought and dollars paid, computes the price of each trade, and then the volume-weighted average, 62,764.71 dollars. A plain average would mislead, because the trade of one bitcoin should count more than the small trade of 0.2. Each trade sets its own price, so everyone who trades moves the day's figure a little.
slides.takeaway: Everyone who trades sets the price a little

slides.title: Two pizzas for ten thousand bitcoin
slides.say: On 22 May 2010 Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoin for two Papa John's pizzas, the first known commercial purchase in bitcoin. He had offered the coins on the bitcointalk forum, and the student Jeremy Sturdivant ordered the pizzas for delivery to Jacksonville. Until then nobody knew what a bitcoin was worth, so this purchase is the day a floating price began to exist. The photograph shows a plaque, and the link leads to the Guinness record. The point is not that the pizzas were worth a lot but that a first price was agreed.
slides.takeaway: 22 May 2010: the day a price began to exist

slides.title: The Pizza Day coins, repriced
slides.say: The same 10,000 coins are priced at six documented moments between 2010 and 2026, and the chart uses a logarithmic axis. The values are 41 dollars, 10,000 dollars, 10 million, 196 million, 690 million and 854 million, so the value grew by a factor of about 20.8 million. A log axis is used because the values span seven orders of magnitude; on a plain axis the early bars would vanish. Price discovery never stopped after the first trade.
slides.takeaway: From 41 dollars to 854 million: price discovery never stopped

slides.title: The network in three beats
slides.say: No bank sits in the middle: shared rules and shared work do its job. This part has three beats. Peers, not a bank: every node checks the same rules, so none is in charge. Work and agreement: proof of work makes an honest history cheap to check and costly to rewrite. Fees and depth: fees pay miners, and each new block makes a payment safer. Slides 29 and 30 cover the peers, slides 31 to 38 work and agreement, and slides 39 to 41 fees and depth. A node is a participant that runs the rules, not a server owned by Bitcoin.
slides.takeaway: No bank sits in the middle: shared rules and shared work do its job.

slides.title: A bank in the middle against peers
slides.say: The slide compares a bank in the middle with peers. On the left one ledger-keeper holds the only ledger, and every account depends on it. On the right every node checks every rule, so no node is in charge. Remove any one node and the network still agrees, which is why decentralisation here is an architecture and not a slogan. The next slides show what the nodes check and how they agree on one history without a leader.
slides.takeaway: Remove any one node and the network still agrees

slides.title: The network: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.say: Three cards define the vocabulary of the network. Proof of work means that adding a block costs real computation while anyone can check it cheaply. Consensus means that every node applies the same rules, so all agree on one history without a leader. A double-spend is spending one unit of digital money twice, and the network refuses the second try. The strip at the bottom shows where this part sits in the chapter. A common error is to think that proof of work solves something useful; its value is the cost itself.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Hard to find, easy to check
slides.say: A toy proof of work searches for a number that makes a hash start with zeros. The result [9, 223, 1208, 57247] gives the guesses needed for one, two, three and four hexadecimal zeros, so each extra zero costs about sixteen times more guesses on average. The chart uses a log axis for this reason. Checking the winner takes one hash instead of the long search. The factor of sixteen is an average over many searches and not an exact ratio for one search.
slides.takeaway: Finding takes thousands of guesses; checking takes one hash

slides.title: Mining pays for honesty
slides.say: Mining pays for honesty. Transactions wait in the mempool, miners spend energy on proof of work, a block is found about every ten minutes, and the reward is the subsidy plus fees. The subsidy follows the halving chart, cheating costs more than it could win, and chapter 12 opens the mechanism. Honest blocks pay in bitcoin, whereas rewriting history would spend the same energy for nothing. Security is bought with energy and paid in bitcoin.
slides.takeaway: Security is bought with energy and paid in bitcoin

slides.title: Keeping blocks ten minutes apart
slides.say: The difficulty adjustment keeps blocks about ten minutes apart whatever the total computing power. After 2016 blocks the network compares the time they took with two weeks and sets the next target to hold ten minutes. If blocks came faster, more computing power joined and the next target needs more leading zeros. If they came slower, the next target is easier. One step changes the difficulty by at most a factor of four. Two weeks of blocks are a measurement, whereas one block is only luck.
slides.takeaway: The network turns its own difficulty dial to hold the pace

slides.title: Why digital money had to wait
slides.say: A digital coin is a file, and files copy perfectly. The four numbered steps on the left lead from digital money to the double-spend. The picture on the right shows one coin reaching two shops as two perfect copies, so both shops see valid money. Before Bitcoin, only a trusted central ledger could stop this. A common mistake is to think that encryption alone prevents copying; it protects secrets but does not stop a valid file from being duplicated.
slides.takeaway: A file can be copied; a coin must not be

slides.title: The double-spend, solved in public
slides.say: The double-spend is solved in public. Every payment is broadcast to every node, the nodes agree on one order for all payments, the first spend of a coin enters the block, and the second is refused by every node. In the picture Alice's coin is paid to Bob first and to Carol second, and the shared ledger keeps only one order. No referee is needed, because agreement on order does the referee's job.
slides.takeaway: Agreement on order is what removes the referee

slides.title: A double spend is refused
slides.say: One shared ledger and one rule refuse a double spend. The code creates a ledger in which coin c1 belongs to Alice, pays it to Bob, and then tries to pay the same coin to Carol. The result {'c1': 'bob'} shows that Carol never receives the coin. Without the rule, both shops would see valid money. In this toy the refusal is a returned text and not an error, and it leaves the owner table unchanged.
slides.takeaway: The second spend of a coin is refused everywhere

slides.title: A chain that notices tampering
slides.say: Each block hashes its text together with the hash of the block before it. The code builds three blocks, checks them, changes the text of block two to 'pay Z' and checks again. The result 1 means that only the first block still checks out, so block two and everything after it are no longer trusted. A common mistake is to think that only the changed block fails; every later link depends on it.
slides.takeaway: Change one old block and every later link fails

slides.title: A chain of dated blocks
slides.say: A block holds a timestamp, a list of transactions and the fingerprint of the block before it, which is why the arrows run backwards. The blockchain is the list of validated blocks, each linking to the one before it back to block 0, and the timestamps place the transactions in an agreed order. Editing block n changes its fingerprint, and every later link breaks. A timestamp orders blocks but does not make their content true; the checks of every node do that.
slides.takeaway: Edit one old block and every later link breaks

slides.title: The network: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.say: Two cards complete the vocabulary of the network. A confirmation is each block added after a payment, and every one makes the payment harder to reverse. A transaction fee is the amount a sender adds for the miner who puts the payment in a block. A payment is not final the moment it is seen, because a later block could still replace it. A common mistake is to confuse the fee with the amount paid to the receiver; the fee is a separate amount.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Each confirmation makes a payment safer
slides.say: A payment is confirmed once when its block is found, and each block built on top adds one more confirmation. To reverse a payment, someone must redo that block and every block after it faster than the honest network adds new ones. Six confirmations at ten minutes a block is about an hour, the usual wait for a larger amount. Card payments and bank transfers can be reversed, whereas a Bitcoin transaction practically cannot. Irreversible here means ever costlier to reverse, not impossible in principle.
slides.takeaway: Irreversible means ever costlier to reverse

slides.title: What the outputs leave over is the fee
slides.say: A transaction has no fee field: the fee is whatever the outputs leave over. One coin of 100,000 satoshis is spent into two outputs of 20,000 and 75,000 satoshis, so the code computes the fee as the sum of the inputs minus the sum of the outputs. The result is 5,000 satoshis, which is 5.0 percent of the coin. The chart shows where the 100,000 satoshis go. A forgotten change output therefore turns into an expensive gift to the miner.
slides.takeaway: The fee is the part of the coin nobody was given

slides.title: Wallets and keys in three beats
slides.say: A wallet holds keys, not coins. This part has three beats: kinds of wallet, nodes and clients, and keys and backup. Desktop, mobile, web and hardware wallets differ in risk. A full node checks everything, while a light client trusts others. Whoever holds the keys controls the coins, and a recovery code restores them. Slides 44 to 46 cover the kinds of wallet, slides 47 and 48 nodes and clients, and slides 49 to 54 keys and backup. Students often picture coins sitting inside the app, but the coins live on the chain.
slides.takeaway: A wallet holds keys, not coins.

slides.title: The wallet branch, mapped
slides.say: Four questions place any wallet on this map: which platform it runs on, which node type it relies on, who controls the keys and how it is backed up. The platform branch lists desktop, mobile, web and hardware signing device. Node type lists full node, lightweight client, third-party API client and peer and client. Key control is noncustodial or custodial, and backup is the recovery code and the wallet metadata. Node type and key control are independent choices, and they are easy to mix up.
slides.takeaway: Four questions place any wallet on this map

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (1 of 4)
slides.say: Four cards open the wallet vocabulary. Getting started covers the first decisions: what a wallet is and which one to choose. Choosing a Bitcoin wallet means picking by who holds the keys, which device it runs on and how far you trust it. The types of Bitcoin wallets are desktop, mobile, web and hardware signing devices, each with its own trade-offs. A desktop wallet is the first kind, run on Windows, macOS or Linux. What makes one kind riskier is who holds the keys and where the device runs.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (2 of 4)
slides.say: Four more kinds of wallet are defined. A mobile wallet is the most common kind and runs on a smartphone. A web wallet is used through a browser, and its data usually sits on someone else's server. A hardware signing device is a small device that keeps keys inside and signs payments. A third-party API client asks a remote service for data instead of the Bitcoin network. A common mistake is to think that a hardware wallet stores coins; it keeps keys and signs, and the coins stay on the chain.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Five kinds of wallet compared
slides.say: The table compares five kinds of wallet: desktop, mobile, web, hardware signing device and third-party API client. Each row names where the keys live and the main risk: malware on the computer, a lost phone with no backup, a host that is hacked or freezes access, a lost device with no recovery code, or a service that sees your questions and may be wrong. The kind of wallet decides who can lose or lock the keys. A hardware wallet holds keys, not coins.
slides.takeaway: The kind of wallet decides who can lose or lock the keys

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (3 of 4)
slides.say: Four cards contrast the ways of running a wallet. A full node is software that checks the whole history of transactions by itself. A lightweight client keeps your keys but relies on other nodes for most of the data. The comparison between them trades independence and storage on one side for convenience and trust on the other. Who controls the keys is the deciding question: whoever holds the private keys controls the coins.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Full node or lightweight client?
slides.say: A full node downloads every block and checks every rule itself. It needs the most storage and time and trusts nobody for the facts. A lightweight client keeps your keys but asks other nodes for most of the data. It needs little storage and starts fast, but it trusts the nodes it asks and may reveal which addresses it watches. Every node is a peer of the others, while a lightweight wallet is a client of one or a few of them. The choice trades independence and some privacy for convenience. A lightweight wallet does keep the keys.
slides.takeaway: Checking for yourself costs storage; asking others costs trust

slides.title: The key alone proves ownership
slides.say: Bitcoin has no registry that names owners. A registered asset is opened by a key, but its owner is recorded in a registry, so losing the key does not change who owns it. In Bitcoin the key does both jobs: signing with the private key is the only proof of ownership there is, and no other record exists to appeal to. A signature proves that you hold the key while the key stays secret. The rule to remember is to prove that you hold the key and never reveal it.
slides.takeaway: Prove you hold the key; never reveal it

slides.title: Whoever holds the keys holds the coins
slides.say: Custody is the first security decision. With full control you keep the keys, you sign, nobody can freeze your coins, and backup is your job. With third-party control a service keeps the keys, which is convenient and custodial but means that you trust its honesty and uptime. The four device labels, desktop, mobile, web and hardware, show where either choice can run. Only the service can freeze coins in the third-party column. Students often underestimate that backup becomes their own job under full control.
slides.takeaway: Custody is the first security decision you make

slides.title: The exchange that lost everyone's coins
slides.say: On 28 February 2014 Mt. Gox of Tokyo, led by Mark Karpeles, filed for bankruptcy at the Tokyo District Court and admitted that about 850,000 bitcoin were gone. Customers had balances on a website, but the keys, and so the coins, were in someone else's hands all along. Creditors were still being repaid a decade later. The logo and the TechCrunch link document the filing. The loss was a loss of custody and not a break of the blockchain: a balance on someone else's website is a promise, not a coin.
slides.takeaway: Tokyo, February 2014: balances on a website, keys elsewhere

slides.title: Where a wallet gets attacked
slides.say: Two common attacks target a wallet. Phishing uses a fake site, message or app that pretends to be your wallet and asks for the recovery code. Malware is a harmful program on your device that reads the wallet data or swaps the address you paste. Three habits help: never type the recovery code into a website, install wallets from the official page, and check the address on a screen you trust. Phishing attacks the person and malware attacks the device. No honest wallet asks for the recovery code in a web form, because anyone who has it owns the coins.
slides.takeaway: No honest wallet asks for the recovery code in a web form

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (4 of 4)
slides.say: Two cards finish the wallet vocabulary. A noncustodial wallet is one where only you hold the keys, so only you can spend or lose the coins. A recovery code is twelve or more words from which all of a wallet's keys can be rebuilt. Twelve words can therefore rebuild every key of the wallet, which is why they must be kept private and offline. A common mistake is to photograph the words and store the picture online.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A recovery phrase becomes a seed
slides.say: A recovery phrase is stretched into a seed. The code splits the BIP 39 test phrase, eleven times abandon and then about, and stretches it with 1, 10 and 2048 rounds of a hash. It prints the first eight hexadecimal digits of each seed: 64d8279a, 297e090a and 5eb00bbd. More rounds give an unrelated seed, and wallets use 2048 rounds, so every guess of an attacker costs 2048 rounds. Slow is deliberate here. The seed is derived from the phrase; it is not the phrase itself.
slides.takeaway: Slow on purpose: every guess costs the full 2048 rounds

slides.title: A first payment in three beats
slides.say: A first payment starts from an empty wallet. This part has three beats: getting bitcoin, addresses and invoices, and receiving and sending. Bitcoin can be bought, earned, or obtained through an exchange or an ATM. An address says where a payment goes, and an invoice adds the amount. Receiving shows an address, while sending signs a transaction. Slides 56 to 60 cover addresses and invoices, and slides 61 to 63 getting bitcoin, receiving and sending. A common slip is to buy bitcoin before the wallet is backed up; the first step is to write down the recovery code.
slides.takeaway: From an empty wallet to a first payment.

slides.title: A first payment: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.say: Four cards define the vocabulary of a first payment. The quick start installs a wallet, shares an address and receives bitcoin. Bitcoin addresses are receiving addresses, and a fresh one for each payer protects privacy. A Bitcoin address is the destination of a payment, derived from your private key and registered nowhere. An invoice is a payment request, often a QR code, that carries an address and an amount. A fresh address for each payer keeps payments from being linked to one another.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Alice's first bitcoin, step by step
slides.say: Alice's first bitcoin takes four steps from an empty phone. She installs a wallet, which makes the keys on her phone. She shares the first address as text or as a QR code. She acquires bitcoin by buying, earning or exchanging. Then the network accepts the payment, and confirmations follow. The wallet writes down a recovery code first, an address is shared with no account opened anywhere, and each confirmation makes the payment harder to reverse. No account is needed because an address is derived from a key and registered nowhere.
slides.takeaway: Four steps from an empty phone to a first payment

slides.title: An address is a hash with a checksum
slides.say: An address is a hash with a checksum. The code builds the address of block 0 in four steps: a version byte, the 20-byte hash of a public key as the payload, a checksum made of the first four bytes of a double SHA-256 of the payload, and the Base58 text of all 25 bytes. The result is the 34-character address 1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa. A mistyped address is caught because the last four bytes check the rest. An address is a hash of the public key, not the key itself.
slides.takeaway: A mistyped address is caught by its checksum

slides.title: An invoice is a link with an amount
slides.say: An invoice is a link with an amount. The code parses a payment request in the form of BIP 21, which packs an address, an amount and a label into one line of text, and converts the amount to satoshis. The result is 15,000 satoshis, because 0.00015 bitcoin is 15,000 satoshis, the figure the wallet shows the payer. The conversion uses exact decimals. A QR code adds nothing to the request: it is the same text drawn as dots.
slides.takeaway: A QR code is only this text, drawn as dots

slides.title: Why one address per payer
slides.say: Reusing an address lets anyone link and total payments. On the left, three payers, Bob, Carol and Dan, all pay address A, so an onlooker can link the three payments and add them up. On the right each payer gets a fresh address, and each payment stands apart from the others. A new address for each payment protects privacy, because an onlooker cannot tell which payments belong to one receiver.
slides.takeaway: A fresh address for each payment keeps payments apart

slides.title: A first payment: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.say: Three cards finish the vocabulary of a first payment. Receiving bitcoin means showing an address or an invoice, and the payment appears once it is broadcast. Getting your first bitcoin means buying from a friend, earning it or using an exchange or an ATM. Sending and receiving differ in that receiving shows an address, while sending signs a transaction to someone else's address. For a student with no bitcoin, buying from a friend is the simplest way.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Four ways to a first bitcoin
slides.say: Four ways lead to a first bitcoin: buy from a friend, earn it, use a Bitcoin ATM or use a currency exchange. The third column says what each way needs from you: an address and an agreed price, an address for the product or service you sell, cash with often an identity check and a fee, or identity verification and a way to pay. Buying from a friend is the simplest; every other way adds a company, a fee or an identity check. A balance at an exchange is not your keys, as the Mt. Gox story shows.
slides.takeaway: Buying from a friend is simplest; an exchange adds identity checks

slides.title: Sending: coins in, payment and change out
slides.say: A wallet spends whole coins and returns the change. The code holds three unspent coins of 50,000, 30,000 and 80,000 satoshis and owes a payment of 60,000 plus a fee of 1,500. It picks the smallest coin that covers both, which is 80,000, because 50,000 does not cover 61,500. The change is 18,500. A coin is spent whole and the change returns as a new output; a coin is never cut.
slides.takeaway: You never cut a coin: you spend it and get change

slides.title: Foundations in three beats
slides.say: Foundations has three beats. Two old solved problems were joined into one system: Hashcash made messages cost work, and the Byzantine generals problem showed how to agree without trust. Payment channels keep most payments off the public ledger. Bitcoin itself is virtual, borderless, decentralized and robust by design. Slides 65 to 69 cover the old problems and the tools, slides 70 to 72 off-chain payments, and slide 73 the kind of thing Bitcoin is. Bitcoin did not solve something that nobody had tried; it joined two solved problems.
slides.takeaway: Two old solved problems, joined into one system.

slides.title: Two solved problems, one new system
slides.say: Two solved problems are joined in one system. Hashcash, from 1997, made sending cost a computation, so that flooding costs real resources; Bitcoin turns the same cost into the price of writing history. The Byzantine generals problem, from 1982, asks how parties that cannot trust each other agree on one message; proof of work plus the longest valid chain is Bitcoin's practical answer. Neither idea was new. Their combination, published in 2008, was.
slides.takeaway: Neither idea was new; their combination was

slides.title: From keys to the chain
slides.say: The pipeline that the rest of the course walks has five stages: keys and addresses in chapter 4, transactions in chapter 6, blocks in chapter 11 and mining in chapter 12. Each stage trusts only what it can verify, and every later chapter opens one of these boxes. This chapter has already touched each box once: an address on slide 58, a transaction with change on slide 63, a chain of blocks on slides 37 and 38, and mining on slide 31. The pipeline is the course syllabus in one row.
slides.takeaway: This pipeline is the course syllabus in one row

slides.title: Five cryptographic tools in a wallet
slides.say: Five cryptographic tools sit inside a wallet. A hash function maps data of any length to a fixed-length fingerprint, and the two real hashes show that one changed character gives an unrelated result. A digital signature is computed from data and a private key and checked with the public key. Public-key cryptography is a pair of related keys. Entropy is unpredictability counted in bits, and twelve words carry 128 bits. A keyed hash mixes in a secret key. A hash has no key, while a keyed hash does.
slides.takeaway: Every wallet builds on these five small ideas

slides.title: Computing words under the chapter
slides.say: Six computing terms sit under this chapter, and the table ties each to where it appears. HTTP and the web browser look up block 0 on mempool.space. The database is what a node uses for blocks and coins and a wallet for labels and history. The operating system is what desktop and mobile wallets run on. A distributed system has no centre, and Bitcoin itself has no central server. Bits and bytes need care, because a 256-bit hash is 32 bytes or 64 hexadecimal digits, and later chapters count in them.
slides.takeaway: Plain computing ideas carry Bitcoin

slides.title: How Bitcoin changes without a boss
slides.say: Bitcoin changes without a boss. An idea for a change becomes a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, a numbered design document discussed in public. The reference implementation, open source software, receives the code, and each node operator decides whether to run it. Anyone may propose, but only the nodes that choose to run a change make it real, so nobody forces an upgrade. Bitcoin Core, descended from Satoshi Nakamoto's 2009 software, is the reference implementation. The W3C row shows the same open habit for identity: open recommendations, decentralized identifiers and verifiable credentials.
slides.takeaway: Anyone may propose; only the nodes that choose to run a change make it real

slides.title: Foundations: the key concepts
slides.say: Offchain technology moves value without recording each payment on the public chain. The picture shows Alice, Bob, Carol and Dave. Alice pays Dave through three channels, and the chain sees nothing of it. The strip at the bottom shows where this part sits in the chapter. A common misconception is that offchain means unsafe. The next slides show that a channel opens and closes on the chain, so its start and end remain public and checkable.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Two transactions, any number of payments
slides.say: A channel costs two transactions on the chain, however many payments follow: one to open and one to close. The code compares payment counts of 1, 10, 100 and 1000 paid on the chain with the same counts paid in a channel, and lists the saving as [-1, 8, 98, 998]. The first value is negative because a single payment alone loses: the channel costs two transactions to serve one payment. A channel pays off from the third payment on.
slides.takeaway: A channel pays off from the third payment on

slides.title: A channel in three steps
slides.say: A payment channel has three steps: open once with one transaction on the chain, pay many times inside the channel with none of those payments reaching the chain, and close once with one transaction. The Lightning Network links channels so that a payment can be routed through several of them; Alice reaches Dave through three channels and the chain sees nothing of it. Offchain payments lower cost and improve privacy, but they change what a backup must cover: the state of the channel as well as the keys.
slides.takeaway: Two transactions on the chain can carry any number of payments

slides.title: What kind of thing is Bitcoin?
slides.say: Bitcoin's stated characteristics are virtual, borderless, decentralized and robust, and each of them is a design choice. The architecture that delivers them has three structures: a peer-to-peer protocol, a public journal and a consensus rule set. The protocol connects the nodes without a centre, the journal keeps the one history that every node can read, and the rule set lets every node check that history for itself. Each adjective is engineered and not only advertised.
slides.takeaway: Each adjective is engineered, not advertised

slides.title: The chapter in six lines
slides.say: The chapter reduces to six lines, one per part. Origins: a dated headline sits in block 0, and the first payment went from person to person. Money: money is a ledger, the cap of 21 million is arithmetic, and the price is discovered by trades. The network has no bank: every node checks every rule, and proof of work makes history costly. A wallet holds keys, not coins. A first payment needs an address or invoice, whole coins, change and a fee. Foundations: two old ideas joined, and payment channels. If a line feels unproven, its code slide carries the evidence.
slides.takeaway: If a line feels unproven, its code slide carries the receipt

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.say: The last content slide collects resources for further reading and watching, and every entry is a live link in this file: the Bitcoin white paper, the first chapter of Mastering Bitcoin, the Bitcoin developer guides, the Bitcoin Core download page, the block explorers mempool.space and blockstream.info, CoinGecko's price data, Bitcoin Stack Exchange, the bitcointalk pizza thread, Adam Back's Hashcash paper, Wei Dai's b-money text and a video by 3Blue1Brown. A good first exercise is to read the white paper and then look up block 0 yourself on mempool.space. The slide was opened on 2026-10-25.

slides.title: What you should now be able to say
slides.say: The closing slide lists what a reader should now be able to say, and where each claim is proved: where Bitcoin came from, why supply is capped and price discovered, how a double spend is refused, and who controls the keys and how a payment works. The six questions from the start of the chapter can each be answered in one sentence. The aim is that every reader can say, in one sentence each, where Bitcoin came from, who holds the keys and how a double spend is refused. Questions are welcome at this point.
